nodes.title: EC2 Auto Scaling groups and capacity

prompts.label: WHAT ARE EC2 AUTO SCALING GROUPS AND CAPACITY SETTINGS?

reveal.text: An EC2 Auto Scaling group maintains instances from a launch template and works toward desired capacity between minimum and maximum bounds.
Use an ASG when EC2 capacity should recover from failures or change with demand.

spans.text: recover from failures or change with demand

reveal.text: If `MaxSize` is 10, a request for 12 instances still stops at 10 because maximum capacity is a hard upper bound.
If scale-out stops early, check maximum capacity and instance-launch errors.

prompts.label: ASG CAPACITY BOUNDS
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Minimum • Desired • Maximum

cells.meaning: Lowest capacity the ASG should maintain.
cells.failure: Unexpected scale-in stops at this floor.
ASG works back toward this number.
Scale-out stops even while demand remains high.

prompts.label: READ THE REAL CONFIG
prompts.placeholder: Key lines: Minimum capacity • Desired capacity • Maximum capacity • Launch template

reveal.code:
Resources:
  WebAsg:
    Type: AWS::AutoScaling::AutoScalingGroup
    Properties:
      MinSize: '2'
      DesiredCapacity: '4'
      MaxSize: '10'
      LaunchTemplate:
        LaunchTemplateId: lt-0123456789abcdef0
        Version: '3'

annotations.title: Minimum capacity
annotations.explanation: The ASG should not intentionally scale below this floor.

annotations.title: Desired capacity
annotations.explanation: The ASG works toward this current target.

annotations.title: Launch template
annotations.explanation: New instances use the referenced launch configuration.

prompts.label: AUTO SCALING OPERATIONAL FEATURES
prompts.placeholder: Compare the main Auto Scaling operational features.

cells.job: Gradually replace instances to roll out a new launch template/configuration
Pause launch or termination so automation can run before the lifecycle continues
cells.clue: Drain, bootstrap, capture logs, or perform custom action

cells.job: Keep pre-initialized instances ready for faster scale-out
cells.clue: Startup time is long and sudden scale-out is too slow

glossary.definition: A reusable EC2 launch configuration that defines settings such as the AMI, instance type, security groups, and other launch options.
An Auto Scaling feature that gradually replaces instances so a group can roll out a new launch template or configuration.
A pause point during instance launch or termination that gives your automation time to run before Auto Scaling continues.
A pool of pre-initialized EC2 instances that can enter an Auto Scaling group faster than launching completely from scratch.
Stop sending new work to a target while allowing existing requests or connections time to finish.

reveal.text: A scaling policy tells Auto Scaling when and how to change capacity.
Use target tracking for a metric target and scheduled scaling for demand at known times.
A weekday 08:00 rush favors scheduled scaling; keeping CPU near 50% favors target tracking.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Target tracking • Step scaling • Scheduled • Predictive

cells.what: Keep a metric near a target
Different adjustments for different breach sizes

cells.use: Recurring patterns where advance capacity helps

reveal.text: Known clock time points to scheduled scaling; a metric target points to target tracking.

prompts.label: HOW IT FLOWS
prompts.placeholder: Flow: Observe demand → … → Warm up and verify

nodes.title: Instance warmup and health-check grace period

prompts.label: WHAT ARE INSTANCE WARMUP AND THE HEALTH-CHECK GRACE PERIOD?

reveal.text: Instance warmup keeps fresh capacity from influencing scaling too soon; health-check grace protects new instances from premature replacement.
Match both settings to real startup behavior to avoid scaling churn or premature replacement.
If a four-minute startup is replaced after one minute, increase the health-check grace period.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Warmup • Health-check grace

cells.use: Avoids reacting too soon to fresh capacity
Avoids terminating instances before the app is ready

reveal.text: New instances replaced before startup completes point to the health-check grace period.

source_refs.title: EC2 Auto Scaling health check grace period
EC2 Auto Scaling default instance warmup

reveal.text: Queue-driven scaling adjusts worker capacity from outstanding work, often using backlog per worker instead of CPU.
Use queue-driven scaling when queued work represents demand better than host utilization.
If the SQS backlog grows while worker CPU stays low, scale on backlog per worker.
A growing queue with low worker CPU points to backlog-based scaling.

prompts.label: SQS QUEUE CHOICES
prompts.placeholder: Compare Standard, FIFO, and dead-letter queue behavior.

cells.behavior: At-least-once delivery; best-effort ordering; very high throughput
cells.use: Order is not strict and consumers are idempotent

cells.behavior: Preserves message-group ordering and supports deduplication/exactly-once processing semantics within SQS constraints
Receives messages that fail processing repeatedly after the configured receive threshold

glossary.definition: Work waiting to be processed, such as messages still waiting in an SQS queue.
Safe to process more than once without changing the final result again. This helps applications handle duplicate messages.
First in, first out. In SQS FIFO queues, messages in the same message group are processed in order.

reveal.text: A CloudFront cache policy controls the cache key and TTLs; an origin request policy forwards extra values without adding them to the cache key.
Keep the cache key as small as correctness allows because unnecessary request values reduce cache hit ratio.
If a tracking query parameter does not change the response, exclude it from the cache key.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Cache policy • Origin request policy

cells.what: Controls cache key and TTL-related behavior
Controls additional request values forwarded to origin
cells.use: Can forward values without putting all of them in the cache key

reveal.text: A low cache-hit ratio from irrelevant query parameters points to removing them from the cache key.

glossary.definition: The request values CloudFront uses to decide whether two requests can use the same cached object.
The backend source CloudFront fetches content from when needed, such as an S3 bucket or a load balancer.
Time to live. It controls how long cached data or a DNS answer can be reused before it should be refreshed.
The share of requests served from cache instead of going back to the origin. A higher ratio usually means less origin work.

prompts.label: HOW DO ELASTICACHE FOR VALKEY/REDIS OSS AND MEMCACHED DIFFER?

reveal.text: Amazon ElastiCache provides managed in-memory caching with Valkey/Redis OSS or Memcached.
Valkey/Redis OSS supports richer data structures and replication; Memcached is a simpler distributed cache.
Replicated cache data with automatic failover favors Valkey/Redis OSS; a disposable simple cache can favor Memcached.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Valkey / Redis OSS • Memcached

cells.what: Rich data structures and replication options
cells.use: Supports HA patterns such as Multi-AZ
Scale-out cache without Redis-style replication model

reveal.text: Replication, failover, or richer data structures point to Valkey/Redis OSS.

prompts.label: DAX VS ELASTICACHE
prompts.placeholder: Compare DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) with ElastiCache.

cells.fit: Microsecond caching for eventually consistent DynamoDB reads with a DynamoDB-compatible API
cells.clue: DynamoDB is the source and read latency must drop to microseconds

cells.fit: General-purpose application/database caching, sessions, rich Redis/Valkey structures, or Memcached
cells.clue: Cache is not specifically a transparent DynamoDB read accelerator

glossary.definition: DynamoDB Accelerator. It is a managed in-memory cache designed to speed up DynamoDB reads.

prompts.label: HOW DO RDS AND AURORA SCALE?

reveal.text: RDS and Aurora scaling can change compute, storage, or read capacity depending on the bottleneck.
Storage pressure points to storage autoscaling; read pressure points to read replicas or Aurora replica scaling.

spans.text: read replicas or Aurora replica scaling

reveal.text: If free storage is nearly exhausted while CPU is low, use storage autoscaling rather than adding a read replica.
Choose the scaling mechanism that matches the constrained resource.
Aurora Serverless v2 automatically scales each serverless writer or reader in ACUs within the cluster's configured capacity range.

glossary.definition: Aurora Capacity Unit. Aurora Serverless v2 uses ACUs to measure and scale database compute and memory capacity.

reveal.text: DynamoDB offers on-demand and provisioned capacity modes for read and write throughput.
Use on-demand for unpredictable traffic; use provisioned with auto scaling when planned throughput fits the workload.
A new ticket-sale workload with unpredictable spikes is a good fit for on-demand capacity.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: On-demand • Provisioned

cells.what: Configured RCU/WCU with optional auto scaling

reveal.text: Highly variable traffic with minimal capacity planning points to on-demand.

glossary.definition: Read Capacity Unit. In DynamoDB provisioned mode, RCUs represent configured read throughput capacity.
Write Capacity Unit. In DynamoDB provisioned mode, WCUs represent configured write throughput capacity.

prompts.label: WHAT ARE ALB, NLB, AND GWLB?

reveal.text: ALB, NLB, and GWLB distribute traffic for different network layers and use cases; ALB and NLB can fail open when no healthy targets remain.
Use ALB for Layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS routing, NLB for Layer 4 TCP/UDP/TLS, and GWLB for virtual network appliances.
Path-based HTTP routing points to ALB; high-throughput TCP without HTTP-aware routing points to NLB.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: ALB • NLB • GWLB

reveal.text: Path-based HTTP routing points to ALB; TCP or UDP transport load balancing points to NLB.

source_refs.title: Health checks for Application Load Balancer target groups
Health checks for Network Load Balancer target groups

glossary.definition: The transport layer. Load balancing here works with protocols such as TCP and UDP instead of HTTP request details.
The application layer. For HTTP and HTTPS, a load balancer can use details such as host names and URL paths.
A load-balancer behavior where traffic can still be sent to unhealthy targets when no healthy targets remain.

nodes.title: Target groups, health checks, deregistration, and cross-zone

prompts.label: HOW DO TARGET HEALTH, DEREGISTRATION, AND CROSS-ZONE LOAD BALANCING WORK?

reveal.text: A target group defines destinations and health checks; deregistration delay gives in-flight work time to drain.
Cross-zone load balancing lets a node use targets in other AZs. ALB has it on at the load-balancer level; NLB has it off by default there.
An unhealthy ALB target leaves normal routing while healthy targets remain; if all registered targets are unhealthy, ALB can fail open.

prompts.label: WHAT HEALTH DATA CAN LOOK LIKE
prompts.placeholder: ALB shows HealthyHostCount=0 while ECS tasks restart: inspect target-health reason and task/container logs.

cells.meaning: No target is currently considered healthy
The app health endpoint is failing
Application startup/readiness is likely the root cause

prompts.label: ELB HEALTH CHECK VS ROUTE 53 HEALTH CHECK
prompts.placeholder: ELB decides whether to send traffic to a target; Route 53 can make DNS routing/failover decisions.

cells.effect: Normally controls target eligibility; ALB can fail open if all targets are unhealthy

cells.scope: DNS endpoint/record health or supported alias target health
cells.effect: Which DNS answer is selected for policies such as failover
cells.example: Primary endpoint unhealthy → answer secondary failover record

reveal.text: A registered target receiving no normal traffic points first to target health and target-group settings.

glossary.definition: A load-balancer behavior where traffic can still be sent to unhealthy targets when no healthy targets remain.
Stop sending new work to a target while allowing existing requests or connections time to finish.

prompts.label: HOW DO ROUTE 53 HEALTH CHECKS AND FAILOVER WORK?

reveal.text: Route 53 can use health checks or Evaluate Target Health when making DNS routing decisions.
Use failover routing for active/passive DNS between a primary and secondary endpoint.
If the primary endpoint becomes unhealthy, failover DNS can answer with the secondary endpoint, subject to DNS caching.
Primary/secondary DNS failover points to Route 53 failover routing.

prompts.label: READ THE REAL CONFIG
prompts.placeholder: Key lines: Primary record • Health evaluation • Secondary record

reveal.code:
Parameters:
  PrimaryHealthCheckId:
    Type: String
  SecondaryHealthCheckId:
    Type: String
Resources:
  PrimaryRecord:
    Type: AWS::Route53::RecordSet
    Properties:
      HostedZoneName: example.com.
      Name: app.example.com.
      Type: A
      TTL: '60'
      ResourceRecords:
        - 192.0.2.10
      SetIdentifier: primary
      Failover: PRIMARY
      HealthCheckId: !Ref PrimaryHealthCheckId
  SecondaryRecord:
    Type: AWS::Route53::RecordSet
    Properties:
      HostedZoneName: example.com.
      Name: app.example.com.
      Type: A
      TTL: '60'
      ResourceRecords:
        - 192.0.2.20
      SetIdentifier: secondary
      Failover: SECONDARY
      HealthCheckId: !Ref SecondaryHealthCheckId

annotations.title: Hosted zone
annotations.explanation: Each record set must identify the hosted zone.

annotations.title: Primary record
annotations.explanation: The primary record is preferred while its health check passes.

annotations.title: Health evaluation
annotations.explanation: The primary record references a Route 53 health check.

annotations.title: Secondary record
annotations.explanation: The secondary record is returned according to failover health behavior.

glossary.definition: Domain Name System. It translates names such as app.example.com into addresses or service endpoints clients can use.

prompts.label: HOW DO RDS MULTI-AZ AND READ REPLICAS DIFFER?

reveal.text: A Multi-AZ DB instance has one non-readable standby; a Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readable standbys. Read replicas mainly scale reads.
Automatic managed failover points to Multi-AZ; additional read capacity points to read replicas.
If the primary fails, a Multi-AZ deployment can fail over for availability; a read replica is mainly for read scaling.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Multi-AZ DB instance • Multi-AZ DB cluster • Read replica

cells.read_behavior: Standby does not serve read traffic
Two standby DB instances can also serve reads
Asynchronous copy used for reads; promotion is a separate action

reveal.text: Automatic failover points to Multi-AZ; scaling read traffic points to a read replica.

prompts.label: WHAT IS A HIGHLY AVAILABLE WEB TIER?

reveal.text: A highly available web tier spreads load balancing, compute, and data across independent failure zones.
Use multi-AZ load balancing, Auto Scaling across AZs, and a highly available data tier.
A multi-AZ ALB, Auto Scaling group, and HA database keep the request path available when one AZ fails.
AZ fault tolerance means avoiding single-AZ dependencies in the request path.

prompts.label: HOW IT FLOWS
prompts.placeholder: Flow: DNS / entry point → … → Highly available data tier

reveal.text: ARC zonal shift moves traffic for supported resources away from an impaired Availability Zone.

nodes.title: AWS Backup plans, vaults, copies, and restore testing

prompts.label: WHAT ARE AWS BACKUP PLANS, VAULTS, COPIES, AND RESTORE TESTING?

reveal.text: AWS Backup centrally manages backup schedules, retention, vault storage, and copy operations for supported resources.

spans.text: schedules, retention, vault storage, and copy operations

reveal.text: Use backup copies for cross-Region or cross-account resilience; restore testing starts scheduled restore jobs and optional validation can check the restored workload.
Monthly restore testing starts real restore jobs from selected recovery points and records completion and duration.
Restore testing proves selected recovery points can complete restore jobs; optional validation checks the restored workload.

prompts.label: AWS BACKUP PARTS
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Backup plan • Backup vault • Copy action • Restore testing

cells.meaning: Schedule, windows, lifecycle, retention, copy rules.
Copies supported backups to another vault/Region/account.

cells.why: Proves recoverability, not just backup success.

prompts.label: READ THE REAL CONFIG
prompts.placeholder: Key lines: Backup plan • Backup vault • Schedule • Lifecycle / retention

reveal.code:
Resources:
  DailyBackupPlan:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupPlan
    Properties:
      BackupPlan:
        BackupPlanName: daily-prod
        BackupPlanRule:
          - RuleName: daily
            TargetBackupVault: prod-vault
            ScheduleExpression: cron(0 5 * * ? *)
            Lifecycle:
              DeleteAfterDays: 35

annotations.title: Backup plan
annotations.explanation: The resource defines centralized backup policy.

annotations.title: Backup vault
annotations.explanation: Recovery points produced by the rule are stored in this vault.

annotations.title: Schedule
annotations.explanation: The rule runs on a defined schedule.

annotations.title: Lifecycle / retention
annotations.explanation: Recovery points are expired according to lifecycle policy.

glossary.definition: How long a backup, recovery point, or other stored data is kept before it can expire or be deleted.

prompts.label: HOW DO EBS SNAPSHOTS AND AMIS DIFFER?

reveal.text: An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time volume backup; an AMI is a launchable EC2 image definition.
Use EBS snapshots for volume restore and AMIs for repeatable instance launches.
A deleted data volume points to an EBS snapshot; launching a known OS/application image points to an AMI.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: EBS snapshot • AMI

cells.what: Launch EC2 instances with an image definition

reveal.text: Creating replacement EC2 instances from a known image points to an AMI.
PITR restores data to a selected time; RDS and DynamoDB restore into a new DB instance or table instead of rewinding the source.
Use PITR for accidental changes or corruption when you need a precise recovery time.
If rows are deleted at 10:17, PITR can restore the 10:16 state into a new resource for validation and cutover.
Recovering the state just before an accidental deletion points to PITR.

nodes.title: S3 replication and FSx recovery features

prompts.label: WHAT ARE S3 REPLICATION AND FSX RECOVERY FEATURES?

reveal.text: Storage recovery can use versioning, replication, backups, snapshots, or service-specific recovery features.
S3 Versioning keeps older object versions; S3 replication copies eligible objects and requires versioning on source and destination buckets.
If an S3 object is overwritten, Versioning can recover a previous object version.

prompts.label: FILE-STORAGE RESILIENCE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: EFS Regional spans AZs; single-AZ designs accept a narrower failure boundary.

cells.example: Shared Linux files must remain available through an AZ failure
cells.tradeoff: Regional EFS stores data across multiple AZs

cells.example: Workload accepts single-AZ resilience for the storage layer
cells.tradeoff: Data is confined to one AZ

cells.example: Managed file service requires automatic failover across AZs
cells.tradeoff: Use the file-system family's HA deployment option

cells.example: Maintain a periodically refreshed second file-system copy
cells.tradeoff: A transfer/copy pattern is not the same thing as synchronous HA

reveal.text: Identify the storage service first because recovery mechanisms are service-specific.
RTO is the maximum acceptable recovery time; RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
Lower RTO needs more ready infrastructure; lower RPO needs more frequent or continuous data protection.
Usable again within 15 minutes means RTO 15 minutes; losing at most 1 minute of data means RPO 1 minute.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: RTO • RPO

cells.what: How long can the service be unavailable?
How much recent data can be lost?

reveal.text: Maximum downtime maps to RTO; maximum acceptable data loss maps to RPO.
Disaster-recovery strategies trade steady-state cost for recovery speed and readiness.
Backup/restore has the least running standby capacity; pilot light keeps core components. Warm standby keeps a reduced functional environment; active/active serves production in multiple locations.
A short recovery time without full production capacity in a second Region is a good fit for warm standby.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Backup & restore • Pilot light • Warm standby • Active/active

reveal.text: Match the DR strategy to RTO, RPO, and cost instead of choosing maximum readiness automatically.

prompts.placeholder: Flow: Define RTO/RPO → … → Test recovery against objectives

prompts.label: STORAGE GATEWAY VS DATASYNC
prompts.placeholder: Compare AWS Storage Gateway with AWS DataSync.

cells.job: Give on-premises applications ongoing file/volume/tape-style access backed by AWS storage
cells.example: Replace physical tape workflow with Tape Gateway

cells.job: Move/copy data between supported on-premises/AWS storage locations
cells.example: Migrate tens of TB from NFS to S3 on a schedule

authoring_notes:
Domain 2 editorial/glossary review: corrected grammar, reduced duplicate teaching, split dense explanations, added beginner-friendly glossary terms, updated selected current AWS behavior, and recalculated coverage counts.

Domain 2 progressive-text pass: all 78 text reveals were shortened into low-friction retrieval prompts. Each uses one hidden key word/phrase normally and never more than two. Surrounding context intentionally makes the answer reasonably guessable. Factual wording was rechecked against current AWS documentation; non-text reveals and curriculum structure remain unchanged.

Glossary migration: glossary terms are now scoped per knowledge node/page instead of globally across the domain. Each page includes only supporting terms actually present in its learner-facing content. The page main topic is not added merely because it is the node title. This avoids irrelevant highlights and context collisions such as treating the words Recovery Point inside RPO as an AWS Backup recovery-point term.
